documents.title: BAD guidelines for biologic therapy for atopic eczema in adults

chunks.content: Introduction AD is an inflammatory skin condition with diverse manifestations stemming from interactions between genetic predispositions and environmental triggers that compromise skin barrier integrity and immune function ( , ). Severe itching is a common symptom that markedly impairs a patient’s quality of life. The incidence rates of AD in adults and children in different countries and regions are 3.4%-33.7% and 13.5%-41.9%, respectively ( , ). Targeted treatments are being developed to improve long-term therapies for patients with moderate-to-severe AD owing to a better understanding of the inflammatory pathways of the disease. Recent studies have identified interleukin-13 (IL-13), a type 2 cytokine, as a crucial factor in AD-related inflammation ( , ). IL-13 is associated with breakdown of the skin barrier, skin inflammation, increased risk of skin infections, itch signaling, and excessive epidermal growth, with IL-13 levels in the affected skin correlating with the severity of AD ( ). Tralokinumab, a fully human IgG4 monoclonal antibody, binds strongly and exclusively to IL-13, blocking its connection with the receptor and the resulting signaling pathways ( ). Tralokinumab demonstrated notable and prompt improvements in the scope and severity of AD in clinical trials involving moderate-to-severe cases, with a safety profile similar to placebo throughout the 52 weeks ( – ). Consequently, they are commonly used in the clinical setting. The most frequent AEs observed with tralokinumab compared with placebo included viral upper respiratory tract infection, upper respiratory tract infection, conjunctivitis, and injection-site reactions ( ). Currently, safety data on tralokinumab are scarce, particularly from large-scale studies and real-world experience. Therefore, it is recommended that post-marketing surveillance of tralokinumab be conducted using data-mining algorithms that comprehensively scan large datasets to detect potential AE signals. Dupilumab, another approved human monoclonal IgG4 antibody, is indicated for the treatment of moderate-to-severe AD and asthma. Dupilumab inhibits the IL-4 and IL-13 signaling pathways by binding to the IL-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Ra), which is shared by the IL-4 and IL-13 receptors, thereby impeding receptor activation and subsequent signaling. Consequently, there is a reduction in epidermal proliferation markers and inflammatory mediators, alongside an increase in structural proteins, lipid metabolism proteins, and epidermal barrier proteins, thereby restoring normal skin function. In this study, we conducted a retrospective analysis of tralokinumab-associated AEs based on the FAERS database. Additionally, our study compared the proportions of injection-site reactions, conjunctivitis, and keratitis reported with tralokinumab and dupilumab. Methods Data source and deduplication We conducted a retrospective pharmacovigilance study analyzing AE data from the FAERS database for the period Q4–2021 to Q2 2025. The FAERS database collects AE reports from a variety of sources, including health professionals, pharmaceutical companies, consumers, and individuals outside the healthcare industry, through spontaneous reporting. Seven datasets categorized FAERS data: demographic and administrative details (DEMO), drug specifics (DRUG), adverse drug reaction details (REAC), patient outcomes (OUTC), sources of reports (RPSR), drug therapy start and end dates (THER), and drug indication information (INDI). Our study adhered to FDA guidelines for data analysis by selecting the most recent entry for each case, based on the latest FDA_DT, when duplicate CASEIDs were present. In addition, if both CASEID and FDA_DT are the same, the entry with the greater PRIMARYID value is selected. This process ensured the exclusion of duplicate data entries, allowing for more accurate assessment of AEs associated with tralokinumab. Following deduplication, we further implemented targeted data cleaning for key variables to address incomplete or implausible records: For age, records with missing values were retained to support descriptive demographic analysis, while implausible entries (e.g., age < 0 or age > 120) were identified and excluded to maintain data validity. Onset time was calculated as the interval between EVENT_DT (adverse event date) and START_DT (tralokinumab initiation date). Reports containing temporal inconsistencies (e.g., EVENT_DT preceding START_DT) or missing medication start/end times were excluded from the analysis. The ROR method was utilized to identify signals of common AEs associated with tralokinumab and dupilumab. AE signals related to the two drugs were compared from each drug’s market authorization through Q2 2025. AEs and drug detection AEs documented in the FAERS database were categorized according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) Information Classification version 27.1. In our study, we identified and analyzed all AEs associated with tralokinumab by extracting data from the ‘REAC’ files within the FAERS database. The analysis focused on evaluating the proportion and severity of AEs using MedDRA SOC and PT categories. To enhance accuracy, we confined our analysis to reports where the drug’s role code was designated as primary suspect (PS) in the DRUG files. To improve the precision of our data analysis, we focused exclusively on adverse reaction reports submitted by medical professionals, identified using the “OCCP_CODE” field in the FAERS database. This field contains codes indicating the reporter’s occupation, allowing us to filter reports submitted by physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and other healthcare professionals. Data mining algorithm Disproportionality analysis was used to evaluate the possible association between tralokinumab and AEs. The study of disproportionality is considered a crucial method in pharmacovigilance research, using four algorithms: the reporting odds ratio (ROR), the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) comprehensive, the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and the multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS). The equations and criteria for the four algorithms have been previously described and are displayed in . One of the four algorithms met these requirements and should be viewed as a promising indicator of drug-associated AEs. For this study, we selected AE signals that satisfied the requirements of the four algorithms discussed earlier. Each obtained AE signal was compared against the drug package insert. If not mentioned in the package insert, the signal was considered an unexpected or novel AE signal. Statistical analysis To further compare the safety profiles of tralokinumab and dupilumab, the chi-square test was used to assess differences in the proportions of selected common AEs, including injection site reactions, conjunctivitis, and keratitis. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. shows the flow chart of our research. RStudio 4.3.2, SPSS 27.0, and Microsoft Excel 2021 were used for all data processing and statistical analyses. Limitations of the study This study has several significant limitations that must be emphasized to ensure proper interpretation of the results. These limitations primarily stem from the inherent characteristics of the FAERS database and restrictions on data completeness. First, FAERS data cannot establish causality; they can only show statistical associations. The pharmacovigilance signals detected in this analysis reflect statistical correlations rather than definitive causal relationships. Second, reporting in FAERS is spontaneous, leading to under-reporting, reporting biases, and the inability to calculate incidence rates. The database captures only the relative frequency of AE reports and lacks incidence or prevalence data from real-world clinical settings. Consequently, associations derived from disproportionality metrics should not be directly extrapolated to clinical incidence rates and should be further validated using complementary data sources. Third, confounding by indication, concomitant medications, and underlying disease severity cannot be controlled for. This severely limits the ability to attribute AEs directly to tralokinumab versus the natural history of severe AD or other treatments. Clinical decision-making should take into account the potential impact of these confounding factors. Results Descriptive analysis From Q4 2021 to Q2 2025, 1,591,367 entries were documented in the FAERS system, with 1,770 reports listing tralokinumab as the PS and 3,137 associated AEs. summarizes the clinical characteristics of tralokinumab-associated events. Females accounted for 62.5% of AE reports, with the majority originating in the United States (93.2%). AD was the most common indication (67.8%), which partially diverged from the labeled indications. Serious outcomes included hospitalization (4.1% of reports), death (1.1% of reports), and life-threatening events (0.3% of reports). Signal detection presents the signal strength and frequency of AEs associated with tralokinumab across different SOCs. While reports covered 25 SOCs, only four showed significant safety signals meeting the criteria for at least one detection method: skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders, general disorders and administration site conditions, eye disorders, and immune system disorders. identifies 49 tralokinumab-related AEs across five SOCs, including labeled events (e.g., conjunctivitis, injection site erythema, and swelling) and unexpected findings (e.g., eczema herpeticum, generalized dermatitis exfoliative, alopecia, skin exfoliation, and blepharitis). Although listed on the drug label, upper respiratory tract infections did not satisfy the criteria for any of the four algorithms assessed. As angioedema and eosinophilia were reported in fewer than three cases, they were not included in the study outcomes. Discussion This study analyzed pharmacovigilance reports of AEs following tralokinumab approval and evaluated the risk of common AEs, including injection site reactions, conjunctivitis, and keratitis, associated with tralokinumab compared with dupilumab. Tralokinumab-related AEs were more prevalent in women than in men (62.5% vs 37.1%), aligning with epidemiological data showing higher AD prevalence in women than in men ( – ). Estradiol and other female hormones may exacerbate Th2 inflammation in patients with AD ( ). The analysis, by SOC, identified the most frequent and clinically significant AEs, including skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders, eye disorders, general disorders and administration site conditions, and immune system disorders. This finding aligns with safety information in the drug label and clinical trials ( , ). AEs related to skin and subcutaneous tissue diseases include rash, erythema, skin burning sensation, and alopecia. Notably, alopecia is not included in the drug label. Alopecia areata is a type 1 autoimmune hair loss disorder, and studies have shown increased Th2-related gene expression in skin biopsies from patients with alopecia, suggesting that dupilumab or tralokinumab may be effective treatments. Research reports indicate that patients receiving tralokinumab or dupilumab may experience worsening or improvement of alopecia symptoms ( – ). It is important to note that the following discussions are speculative hypotheses, as the exact mechanisms underlying the association between these drugs and alopecia remain unclear. Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain dupilumab-induced alopecia, ranging from disease exacerbation to therapeutic improvement ( , ). One line of reasoning suggests that Th2 cell inhibition may inadvertently upregulate alternative immune pathways, particularly the Th1/Th17 axis, which is known to drive alopecia areata pathogenesis ( ). In contrast, another perspective posits that dupilumab’s blockade of IL-4 signaling could dampen the production of pro-inflammatory mediators, potentially concurrently ameliorating both alopecia and AD manifestations ( ). A third hypothesis proposes that IL-4 and IL-13 expression correlate positively with sebaceous gland function, and reduced activity of these cytokines may disrupt glandular development, leading to atrophy and secondary alopecia areata ( ). Furthermore, studies have found that features of alopecia areata are associated with the activation of TH1, TH2, IL-23, and IL-9/TH9 cytokines ( ). Future clinical trials of selective antagonists are needed to identify key pathogenic pathways and validate these hypotheses. Beyond cutaneous manifestations, infectious complications represent another critical safety consideration. Infection-related AEs include eczema herpeticum (a cutaneous infection caused by HSV), conjunctivitis, and other ocular infections. Notably, eczema herpeticum is not listed in tralokinumab’s adverse reaction profile, despite a 0.3%–0.5% incidence in phase III trials—lower than the control group ( , ). However, it is essential to note that eczema herpeticum may represent a manifestation or complication of severe AD rather than an accurate drug-related AE. Tralokinumab’s specific binding to IL-13 (without affecting IL-4) may contribute to this low risk, though the exact mechanism remains unclear. Proposed pathways include decreased expression of keratinocyte/tight junction proteins (e.g., claudins), impairing skin barrier integrity; reduced interferon/antimicrobial peptide production; and a predominantly Th2 immune response with abnormal regulatory T cell levels—all of which increase HSV susceptibility ( ). Ocular AEs constitute a significant safety concern associated with tralokinumab, with conjunctivitis being the most commonly reported event. Five randomized controlled trials demonstrated a 7.5% incidence of conjunctivitis in tralokinumab-treated patients compared to 3.2% in placebo-treated patients ( ), and a meta-analysis confirmed a significantly elevated risk with tralokinumab ( ). Notably, our study revealed that the proportion of tralokinumab-related conjunctivitis was considerably higher than that of dupilumab (2.4% vs. 1.4%, p=0.001). It should be emphasized that these percentages represent the proportion of reports, not the proportion of patients or the true incidence of these events. Risk factors for severe conjunctivitis include baseline AD severity, history of allergic conjunctivitis, atopic keratoconjunctivitis, and multiple atopic comorbidities ( ). It is important to note that FAERS-based comparisons do not reflect accurate incidence rates, as they are subject to reporting biases and other limitations. Therefore, the higher reporting proportion of conjunctivitis with tralokinumab compared with dupilumab should be interpreted with caution and may not represent an actual difference in incidence. The pathophysiology of biologic agent-related ocular AEs involves IL-4/IL-13-mediated disruption of conjunctival homeostasis. Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-4/IL-13 (through IL-4Rα interaction) inhibit conjunctival goblet cell activation, decrease mucin secretion, and compromise tear film stability ( , ). This cascade results in dysfunction of the mucosal epithelial barrier and subsequent ocular inflammation. Mechanistic explanations for these findings remain highly speculative and require further investigation. Specifically for tralokinumab, it is hypothesized that its selective inhibition of IL-13 may partially reduce this risk compared to dual IL-4/IL-13 inhibitors, based on current knowledge of IL-13’s role in ocular inflammation. However, this hypothesis is not directly supported by our FAERS-based finding that the reporting proportion of tralokinumab-related conjunctivitis was significantly higher than that of dupilumab. This discrepancy highlights the limitations of FAERS data for comparing the safety profiles of different biologic agents and the need for caution when interpreting such results. Further research is required to elucidate the relationship between tralokinumab’s selective IL-13 inhibition and the risk of ocular AEs, and to identify potential confounding factors that may account for the higher reporting proportion of conjunctivitis with tralokinumab compared to dupilumab. Clinical management of tralokinumab-associated ocular AEs should follow a stepwise approach. Clinicians should assess symptom severity and initiate topical lubricants or antihistamine drops for mild cases. Persistent symptoms warrant referral to ophthalmology for slit-lamp examination and potential topical corticosteroid therapy. Close monitoring is critical, as untreated ocular inflammation may progress to keratitis or vision impairment. Other ocular AEs include eyelid irritation, eye pain, eye swelling, eye discharge, dry eye, ocular hyperemia, increased lacrimation, and blepharitis. Except for blepharitis, these reflect manifestations of conjunctivitis. Blepharitis, unlabeled for tralokinumab, has been reported with both biologics (8% incidence with dupilumab) ( ). Studies suggest that by binding to IL-4Rα and thereby inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13, these monoclonal antibodies prevent conjunctival goblet cell activation, leading to hypoplasia and decreased mucin production, which, in turn, affects the stability of the tear film and the function of the mucosal epithelial barrier ( ). To our knowledge, there are currently no reports of visual impairment associated with tralokinumab, whereas several studies have reported visual impairment and blurred vision with dupilumab ( , ). This study identified a signal for blurred vision AEs related to tralokinumab treatment. Therefore, it is essential to consult an ophthalmologist promptly when visual issues arise during treatment to minimize potential vision damage. Our study also identified several AEs in the SOC of general disorders and administration site conditions, including injection site pain, injection site erythema, swelling, and rash at the injection site, as well as facial swelling. All these AEs have been documented in the medication instructions. Our research indicates that the risk of injection site reactions (including pain, swelling, and cyanosis) associated with dupilumab is significantly higher than that associated with tralokinumab (21.3% vs. 15.6%, p<0.001). Urticaria is an AE not listed on the drug label. At present, studies are reporting AE of urticaria caused by treatment with dupilumab ( ). The exact pathogenesis of urticaria remains incompletely understood, but it typically involves the release of various mediators from mast cells, such as histamine, proteases, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines ( ). Exfoliative dermatitis is a severe form of dermatitis that can be caused by a variety of factors, including underlying skin diseases, infections, and medications ( ). Therefore, the occurrence of exfoliative dermatitis in patients treated with tralokinumab may be related to underlying disease severity rather than to the treatment itself. Further research is required to elucidate the relationship between tralokinumab treatment and the risk of exfoliative dermatitis. These findings emphasize the necessity for dermatologists to enhance patient monitoring and education throughout the treatment process. Our results demonstrated that the median time to onset of tralokinumab-related AEs was 37 days, with most occurring within the first month of treatment. Conclusion This study conducted a comprehensive pharmacovigilance analysis of tralokinumab-associated AEs using FAERS data, identifying potential safety signals not listed on the product label: eczema herpeticum, generalized exfoliative dermatitis, hair loss, skin exfoliation, and eyelid inflammation. Notably, eczema herpeticum, generalized exfoliative dermatitis, and skin exfoliation may reflect severe AD manifestations rather than true drug-related AEs, highlighting the risk of misclassifying disease vs. treatment-related events. Comparative analysis with dupilumab revealed differential AE profiles: dupilumab had higher injection-site reaction reporting rates, while tralokinumab showed higher conjunctivitis and keratitis rates. These findings inform post-market safety monitoring and clinical decision-making by highlighting underrecognized tralokinumab-associated AEs requiring closer monitoring. However, results should be interpreted cautiously due to limitations in the FAERS database (reporting biases and underreporting) and the observational study design. This study generates hypotheses that require validation through well-designed clinical trials to confirm safety signals, establish causal relationships, and characterize tralokinumab’s safety profile. Prospective trials with rigorous designs and larger sample sizes are needed to determine the accurate AE incidence rates, while mechanistic studies should elucidate underlying pathways and risk factors.

Introduction Psoriasis is a chronic disease caused by an inflammatory condition of the skin, sometimes associated with other conditions such as psoriatic arthritis, psychological, cardiovascular, and gastrointestinal disorders. The World Health Organization (WHO) [ ] has considered psoriasis a serious non-communicable disease and has emphasized the importance of appropriate clinical treatments, which are often compromised due to frequent misdiagnosis [ ]. Psoriasis occurs in both sexes but tends to manifest earlier in women and in those with a family history of the disease. The age of onset usually falls within two decades: between 30 and 39 years and between 60 and 69 years for men, whereas in women, the first symptoms may appear up to 10 years earlier [ , ]. The clinical manifestations of psoriasis are heterogeneous and include cutaneous and systemic manifestations [ , ]. Most commonly, psoriasis presents as plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris), occurring in 80% of cases [ , ]. Symptoms include itching, burning sensations, and skin tenderness [ , ]. Several comorbidities are associated with psoriasis, including psoriatic arthritis, cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, obesity, and inflammatory bowel disease [ , , ]. Due to these systemic implications, psoriasis is also referred to as a systemic disease [ ], a pathology linked to skin barrier dysfunction [ ] and metabolic syndrome [ ]. The etiology of psoriasis is complex and encompasses many intrinsic and extrinsic factors [ , , , , ]. Psoriasis is mainly characterized by the activation of inflammatory pathways in innate and adaptive immune cells, leading to uncontrolled keratinocyte (KC) proliferation, acanthosis, neovascularization, and dense infiltration of immune cells into the skin [ ]. Pro-inflammatory cytokines primarily involved in the pathogenesis of psoriasis are mainly produced by T cells (e.g., IL-17, IL-21, IL-22, IFN-γ) and dendritic cells (DCs; e.g., TNF-α, IL-6, IL-20, IL-23, NO), forming a central pathogenic loop with IL-23-producing dendritic cells, IL-17-producing Th17 cells, and activated keratinocytes (KCs) [ , , , ]. TNF-α initiates the inflammatory cascade in psoriasis. It is secreted in response to triggers such as skin lesions, environmental stimuli, auto-antigens, and TLR receptor agonists [ , ], mainly by activated T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs) [ , ]. TNF-α synergizes with IFN-γ to induce chemokine expression in endothelial cells, promoting immune cell infiltration [ , ] and stimulating KCs and DCs to secrete IL-23 [ ]. Accordingly, the results of numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) and clinical trials support the central role of the inflammatory signaling molecular pathways of TNF-α, IL-23, and IL-17 as the “founding fathers” of the pathogenesis of psoriasis, particularly plaque psoriasis [ , , , ]. Both the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the European Medicine Agency (EMA) have approved different monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) for treating plaque psoriasis, targeting TNF-α (e.g., adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab) [ , ], IL-23 (e.g., risankizumab, tildrakizumab, guselkumab) [ , ], and IL-17 (e.g., secukinumab, brodalumab, bimekizumab, ixekinumab) [ , , ]. These agents achieve PASI 90 and PASI 100 response rates between 67% and 89% [ ]. Because of this extensive range of options, several international consensus guidelines support a personalized approach to care [ , , , , , , ], accounting for disease phenotype, treatment history, comorbidities (e.g., IBD, demyelinating disease, drug characteristics (e.g., administration route, frequency), and lifestyle factors (e.g., family planning) [ , , , , , , ]. For instance, genomic data, particularly the HLA*C60:02 status, may also guide treatment selection [ ]; HLA*C60:02-negative patients tend to respond better to anti-TNF-α than anti-IL12/23 agents [ ]. Furthermore, the availability of administration routes that do not require the assistance of specialized healthcare personnel, such as subcutaneous formulations or oral options, may offer a practical advantage for simplifying clinical management and improving patient convenience [ ]. Real-world evidence (RWE) from immune-mediated diseases, including inflammatory bowel diseases (IBDs), Spondyloarthritis (SpA), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and chronic plaque psoriasis (PsO), supports the clinical utility of SC infliximab, showing high treatment persistence, stable disease control, and favorable safety profiles in routine practice, together with improvements in convenience and patient experience [ , , , , , , , ]. Notably, these effects are likely attributable to the stable pharmacokinetic profile of the subcutaneous formulation, characterized by high Ctrough values and reduced immunogenicity [ ]. These data reinforce the rationale for evaluating an IV-to-SC transition in plaque psoriasis, where comparable benefits, particularly around convenience and adherence, may be clinically meaningful. Study Population Data were collected between December 2023 and January 2024 and entered in an ad hoc database containing anonymized clinical and personal data. Anonymization was ensured through the immediate generation of an encrypted code, guaranteeing patient confidentiality. 2.2. Clinical Condition, Comorbidities, and Data Recovery Data from 11 patients were entered into our database for statistical analysis. All patients had moderate to severe plaque psoriasis vulgaris. The patient group for these analyses consisted of 6 females and 5 males. The mean age was 45.5 ± 18.2 years. The diagnosis of plaque psoriasis was made at a specialized dermatology center. All patients were referred for systemic treatment, and each patient received intravenous IFX prior to transitioning to subcutaneous IFX administration. No other treatments, either concurrent or alternative, were administered. Only one patient (ID 4) in this case series presented with comorbid psoriatic arthritis. 2.3. Treatment All patients had previously failed one or more courses of traditional systemic therapies (e.g., retinoids, cyclosporine, methotrexate) and subsequently began therapy with intravenous IFX at a dose of 5 mg/kg, with a mean treatment duration of 20 months (range: 9–38 months). According to the product information, transition to SC IFX therapy can begin from the sixth week of therapy, following two intravenous IFX infusions—one at initiation and one after two weeks. In this case series, all patients received intravenous IFX administered by trained personnel. Thereafter, SC-IFX was self-administered by the patients themselves, as reported in the literature [ ]. All patients transitioned to SC-IFX after a mean of 20–27 months of intravenous IFX and continued SC therapy for 12 months. 2.4. TSQM-9 Questionnaire Patient satisfaction with their pharmacological treatment was assessed using the Treatment Satisfaction Questionnaire Medication-9 (TSQM-9). The questionnaire consists of 9 questions covering various aspects of treatment and offers single-choice, multiple-option answers on Likert scales (only one answer is selectable). Seven of the nine questions use a 7-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (bad) to 7 (good), while two questions (Q7 and Q8) use a 5-point Likert scale, ranging from 1 (bad) to 5 (good). Lower scores correspond to worse impressions, while higher scores are associated with better impressions. The total score of the questionnaire ranges from 9 (minimum) to 59 (maximum) points. A total score of 50 points indicates a high level of patient satisfaction (HLS). However, based on procedures reported in the scientific literature, TSQM-9 results are expressed as percentages (0–100%) to allow for data normalization [ ]. Patient-reported scores were normalized by expressing the maximum questionnaire score (59 points) as 100%. Indeed, TSQM-9 values ≥50 points (84.75%) were selected as the threshold for HLS. TSQM-9 data were collected at the end of IV-IFX treatment and after 12 months of SC-IFX treatment. 2.5. PASI, DLQI, and PGAs The Psoriasis Area and Severity Index (PASI), Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI), and Physician Global Assessment (PGA) scores were assessed before and after SC-IFX treatment. The PASI (0–72), DLQI (0–30) and the PGA (0, clear; 1, almost clear; 2, mild; 3, moderate; and 4, severe; ) scores recorded by the patient were assessed by the attending physician at SC-IFX treatment initiation and 48 weeks after SC-IFX treatment [ ]. 2.6. Statistical Analyses Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad 8.0 version (PRISM, San Diego, CA, USA). The Shapiro–Wilk test was applied to determine whether the data were parametrically distributed. Both W- and p -values were calculated. Student’s t-Test (parametric and paired) was used to compare TSQM-9 after IV-IFX (0 weeks) and SC-IFX (48 weeks) visits. Student’s t-Test was used to compare TSQM-9 scores, their normalized values (expressed as percentages), and delta variations between both treatments relative to the HLS reference point. In addition, ANOVA was used to compare TSQM scores between IV and SC–IFX treatments. All results are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD) and number of items (N). For all quantitative analyses, statistical significance was defined as a p -value less than 0.05 ( p < 0.05, *: p < 0.01, **; p < 0.001, ***; and p < 0.0001, ****). 3. Results 3.1. Follow-Up and Treatments All patients demonstrated full treatment compliance with SC-IFX self-injections, and all completed at least 12 months of follow-up. The mean total treatment time (TTT; IV + SC) was 32.4 months (22 ÷ 50 months). Both PASI ( A) and DLQI ( B) improved at follow-up: the mean PASI decreased by approximately 10% after SC treatment, and DLQI improved in 100% of patients.

With respect to the HLS threshold, the deltas were −15.9% ± 4.4 for IV-IFX and 8.6% ± 3.2 for SC-IFX with a mean between-treatment difference of 24.5% ( p < 0.0001; C). Considering all items (Q1-Q9), the ANOVA results indicate significant effects of treatment (IV vs. SC; p < 0.0001) and differences in item scores ( p < 0.0001). Sidak post hoc testing identified significant differences in 6 of 9 items: Q1 ( p < 0.05), Q3 ( p < 0.01), Q4 ( p < 0.0001), Q5 ( p < 0.0001), Q6 ( p < 0.0001), and Q9 ( p < 0.0001). Notably, Q4 to Q6, which assess treatment management/convenience, favored SC-IFX treatment, with mean differences of 3.545, 3.182, and 3.273 for Q4, Q5, and Q6, respectively ( p < 0.0001; D). 3.3. PGA PGA score analysis showed an improvement, indicating an added benefit of SC-IFX. The proportion of patients who rated clear (score 0) versus almost clear (score 1) was 8:3 during IV treatment and 10:1 after SC treatment. This pattern reflects an interesting trend: SC-IFX did not worsen treatment clinical status and was rather associated with improvement in 18.2% of subjects ( and ). 3.4. Furthermore, in our study, the TSQM-9 results also surpassed the high-level satisfaction (HLS) threshold, both in absolute score (50/59 points) and percentage (84.74%). ANOVA analysis showed that items Q4, Q5, and Q6, which reflect “treatment management/convenience” from the patient’s point of view [ ], were 3-points higher on average with SC-IFX than those registered for IV-IFX ( p < 0.001; D). Although we did not perform pharmacokinetic or immunogenicity assessments in our cohort, phase I–III bridging studies comparing SC-IFX with its intravenous formulation have shown higher and more stable trough serum concentrations with SC administration, while maintaining comparable efficacy, safety, and overall rates of anti-drug antibodies [ , , ]. This pattern has been interpreted as compatible with a high-zone tolerance mechanism, whereby sustained higher drug exposure does not increase, and may attenuate, clinically relevant immunogenic responses [ ]. This pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity profile provides a mechanistic rationale for our observation that switching from IV to SC infliximab maintained clinical remission in patients with psoriasis. Intriguingly, the recent REWATCH study provides reassuring data that earlier switching from IV- to SC-IFX does not compromise efficacy and safety in IBD patients [ ]. Further evidence is needed to explore this hypothesis in the context of other chronic immune-mediated diseases. TSQM-9 scores revealed a greater treatment satisfaction with SC-IFX, particularly regarding convenience and daily treatment management. The results suggest that switching to subcutaneous IFX therapy did not worsen clinical assessment scores or raise safety concerns, supporting SC-IFX as a valid and apparently safe maintenance option after prior exposure to IV-IFX. chunks.content: Introduction AD is an inflammatory skin condition with diverse manifestations stemming from interactions between genetic predispositions and environmental triggers that compromise skin barrier integrity and immune function ( , ). Severe itching is a common symptom that markedly impairs a patient’s quality of life. The incidence rates of AD in adults and children in different countries and regions are 3.4%-33.7% and 13.5%-41.9%, respectively ( , ). Targeted treatments are being developed to improve long-term therapies for patients with moderate-to-severe AD owing to a better understanding of the inflammatory pathways of the disease. Recent studies have identified interleukin-13 (IL-13), a type 2 cytokine, as a crucial factor in AD-related inflammation ( , ). IL-13 is associated with breakdown of the skin barrier, skin inflammation, increased risk of skin infections, itch signaling, and excessive epidermal growth, with IL-13 levels in the affected skin correlating with the severity of AD ( ). Tralokinumab, a fully human IgG4 monoclonal antibody, binds strongly and exclusively to IL-13, blocking its connection with the receptor and the resulting signaling pathways ( ). Tralokinumab demonstrated notable and prompt improvements in the scope and severity of AD in clinical trials involving moderate-to-severe cases, with a safety profile similar to placebo throughout the 52 weeks ( – ). Consequently, they are commonly used in the clinical setting. The most frequent AEs observed with tralokinumab compared with placebo included viral upper respiratory tract infection, upper respiratory tract infection, conjunctivitis, and injection-site reactions ( ). Currently, safety data on tralokinumab are scarce, particularly from large-scale studies and real-world experience. Therefore, it is recommended that post-marketing surveillance of tralokinumab be conducted using data-mining algorithms that comprehensively scan large datasets to detect potential AE signals. Dupilumab, another approved human monoclonal IgG4 antibody, is indicated for the treatment of moderate-to-severe AD and asthma. Dupilumab inhibits the IL-4 and IL-13 signaling pathways by binding to the IL-4 receptor alpha subunit (IL-4Ra), which is shared by the IL-4 and IL-13 receptors, thereby impeding receptor activation and subsequent signaling. Consequently, there is a reduction in epidermal proliferation markers and inflammatory mediators, alongside an increase in structural proteins, lipid metabolism proteins, and epidermal barrier proteins, thereby restoring normal skin function. In this study, we conducted a retrospective analysis of tralokinumab-associated AEs based on the FAERS database. Additionally, our study compared the proportions of injection-site reactions, conjunctivitis, and keratitis reported with tralokinumab and dupilumab. Methods Data source and deduplication We conducted a retrospective pharmacovigilance study analyzing AE data from the FAERS database for the period Q4–2021 to Q2 2025. The FAERS database collects AE reports from a variety of sources, including health professionals, pharmaceutical companies, consumers, and individuals outside the healthcare industry, through spontaneous reporting. Seven datasets categorized FAERS data: demographic and administrative details (DEMO), drug specifics (DRUG), adverse drug reaction details (REAC), patient outcomes (OUTC), sources of reports (RPSR), drug therapy start and end dates (THER), and drug indication information (INDI). Our study adhered to FDA guidelines for data analysis by selecting the most recent entry for each case, based on the latest FDA_DT, when duplicate CASEIDs were present. In addition, if both CASEID and FDA_DT are the same, the entry with the greater PRIMARYID value is selected. This process ensured the exclusion of duplicate data entries, allowing for more accurate assessment of AEs associated with tralokinumab. Following deduplication, we further implemented targeted data cleaning for key variables to address incomplete or implausible records: For age, records with missing values were retained to support descriptive demographic analysis, while implausible entries (e.g., age < 0 or age > 120) were identified and excluded to maintain data validity. Onset time was calculated as the interval between EVENT_DT (adverse event date) and START_DT (tralokinumab initiation date). Reports containing temporal inconsistencies (e.g., EVENT_DT preceding START_DT) or missing medication start/end times were excluded from the analysis. The ROR method was utilized to identify signals of common AEs associated with tralokinumab and dupilumab. AE signals related to the two drugs were compared from each drug’s market authorization through Q2 2025. AEs and drug detection AEs documented in the FAERS database were categorized according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) Information Classification version 27.1. In our study, we identified and analyzed all AEs associated with tralokinumab by extracting data from the ‘REAC’ files within the FAERS database. The analysis focused on evaluating the proportion and severity of AEs using MedDRA SOC and PT categories. The study of disproportionality is considered a crucial method in pharmacovigilance research, using four algorithms: the reporting odds ratio (ROR), the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA) comprehensive, the Bayesian confidence propagation neural network (BCPNN), and the multi-item gamma Poisson shrinker (MGPS). The equations and criteria for the four algorithms have been previously described and are displayed in . One of the four algorithms met these requirements and should be viewed as a promising indicator of drug-associated AEs. For this study, we selected AE signals that satisfied the requirements of the four algorithms discussed earlier. Each obtained AE signal was compared against the drug package insert. If not mentioned in the package insert, the signal was considered an unexpected or novel AE signal. Statistical analysis To further compare the safety profiles of tralokinumab and dupilumab, the chi-square test was used to assess differences in the proportions of selected common AEs, including injection site reactions, conjunctivitis, and keratitis. A p-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. shows the flow chart of our research. RStudio 4.3.2, SPSS 27.0, and Microsoft Excel 2021 were used for all data processing and statistical analyses. Limitations of the study This study has several significant limitations that must be emphasized to ensure proper interpretation of the results. These limitations primarily stem from the inherent characteristics of the FAERS database and restrictions on data completeness. First, FAERS data cannot establish causality; they can only show statistical associations. The pharmacovigilance signals detected in this analysis reflect statistical correlations rather than definitive causal relationships. Second, reporting in FAERS is spontaneous, leading to under-reporting, reporting biases, and the inability to calculate incidence rates. The database captures only the relative frequency of AE reports and lacks incidence or prevalence data from real-world clinical settings. Consequently, associations derived from disproportionality metrics should not be directly extrapolated to clinical incidence rates and should be further validated using complementary data sources. Third, confounding by indication, concomitant medications, and underlying disease severity cannot be controlled for. This severely limits the ability to attribute AEs directly to tralokinumab versus the natural history of severe AD or other treatments. Clinical decision-making should take into account the potential impact of these confounding factors. Tralokinumab-related AEs were more prevalent in women than in men (62.5% vs 37.1%), aligning with epidemiological data showing higher AD prevalence in women than in men ( – ). Estradiol and other female hormones may exacerbate Th2 inflammation in patients with AD ( ). The analysis, by SOC, identified the most frequent and clinically significant AEs, including skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders, eye disorders, general disorders and administration site conditions, and immune system disorders. This finding aligns with safety information in the drug label and clinical trials ( , ). AEs related to skin and subcutaneous tissue diseases include rash, erythema, skin burning sensation, and alopecia. Notably, alopecia is not included in the drug label. Alopecia areata is a type 1 autoimmune hair loss disorder, and studies have shown increased Th2-related gene expression in skin biopsies from patients with alopecia, suggesting that dupilumab or tralokinumab may be effective treatments. Research reports indicate that patients receiving tralokinumab or dupilumab may experience worsening or improvement of alopecia symptoms ( – ). It is important to note that the following discussions are speculative hypotheses, as the exact mechanisms underlying the association between these drugs and alopecia remain unclear. Several hypotheses have been proposed to explain dupilumab-induced alopecia, ranging from disease exacerbation to therapeutic improvement ( , ). One line of reasoning suggests that Th2 cell inhibition may inadvertently upregulate alternative immune pathways, particularly the Th1/Th17 axis, which is known to drive alopecia areata pathogenesis ( ). In contrast, another perspective posits that dupilumab’s blockade of IL-4 signaling could dampen the production of pro-inflammatory mediators, potentially concurrently ameliorating both alopecia and AD manifestations ( ). A third hypothesis proposes that IL-4 and IL-13 expression correlate positively with sebaceous gland function, and reduced activity of these cytokines may disrupt glandular development, leading to atrophy and secondary alopecia areata ( ). Furthermore, studies have found that features of alopecia areata are associated with the activation of TH1, TH2, IL-23, and IL-9/TH9 cytokines ( ). Future clinical trials of selective antagonists are needed to identify key pathogenic pathways and validate these hypotheses. Beyond cutaneous manifestations, infectious complications represent another critical safety consideration. Infection-related AEs include eczema herpeticum (a cutaneous infection caused by HSV), conjunctivitis, and other ocular infections. Notably, eczema herpeticum is not listed in tralokinumab’s adverse reaction profile, despite a 0.3%–0.5% incidence in phase III trials—lower than the control group ( , ). However, it is essential to note that eczema herpeticum may represent a manifestation or complication of severe AD rather than an accurate drug-related AE. Tralokinumab’s specific binding to IL-13 (without affecting IL-4) may contribute to this low risk, though the exact mechanism remains unclear. Proposed pathways include decreased expression of keratinocyte/tight junction proteins (e.g., claudins), impairing skin barrier integrity; reduced interferon/antimicrobial peptide production; and a predominantly Th2 immune response with abnormal regulatory T cell levels—all of which increase HSV susceptibility ( ). Ocular AEs constitute a significant safety concern associated with tralokinumab, with conjunctivitis being the most commonly reported event. Five randomized controlled trials demonstrated a 7.5% incidence of conjunctivitis in tralokinumab-treated patients compared to 3.2% in placebo-treated patients ( ), and a meta-analysis confirmed a significantly elevated risk with tralokinumab ( ). Notably, our study revealed that the proportion of tralokinumab-related conjunctivitis was considerably higher than that of dupilumab (2.4% vs. 1.4%, p=0.001). It should be emphasized that these percentages represent the proportion of reports, not the proportion of patients or the true incidence of these events. The pathophysiology of biologic agent-related ocular AEs involves IL-4/IL-13-mediated disruption of conjunctival homeostasis. Monoclonal antibodies targeting IL-4/IL-13 (through IL-4Rα interaction) inhibit conjunctival goblet cell activation, decrease mucin secretion, and compromise tear film stability ( , ). This cascade results in dysfunction of the mucosal epithelial barrier and subsequent ocular inflammation. Mechanistic explanations for these findings remain highly speculative and require further investigation. Specifically for tralokinumab, it is hypothesized that its selective inhibition of IL-13 may partially reduce this risk compared to dual IL-4/IL-13 inhibitors, based on current knowledge of IL-13’s role in ocular inflammation. However, this hypothesis is not directly supported by our FAERS-based finding that the reporting proportion of tralokinumab-related conjunctivitis was significantly higher than that of dupilumab. This discrepancy highlights the limitations of FAERS data for comparing the safety profiles of different biologic agents and the need for caution when interpreting such results. Further research is required to elucidate the relationship between tralokinumab’s selective IL-13 inhibition and the risk of ocular AEs, and to identify potential confounding factors that may account for the higher reporting proportion of conjunctivitis with tralokinumab compared to dupilumab. Clinical management of tralokinumab-associated ocular AEs should follow a stepwise approach. Clinicians should assess symptom severity and initiate topical lubricants or antihistamine drops for mild cases. Persistent symptoms warrant referral to ophthalmology for slit-lamp examination and potential topical corticosteroid therapy. Close monitoring is critical, as untreated ocular inflammation may progress to keratitis or vision impairment. Other ocular AEs include eyelid irritation, eye pain, eye swelling, eye discharge, dry eye, ocular hyperemia, increased lacrimation, and blepharitis. Except for blepharitis, these reflect manifestations of conjunctivitis. Blepharitis, unlabeled for tralokinumab, has been reported with both biologics (8% incidence with dupilumab) ( ). Studies suggest that by binding to IL-4Rα and thereby inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13, these monoclonal antibodies prevent conjunctival goblet cell activation, leading to hypoplasia and decreased mucin production, which, in turn, affects the stability of the tear film and the function of the mucosal epithelial barrier ( ). To our knowledge, there are currently no reports of visual impairment associated with tralokinumab, whereas several studies have reported visual impairment and blurred vision with dupilumab ( , ). This study identified a signal for blurred vision AEs related to tralokinumab treatment. Therefore, it is essential to consult an ophthalmologist promptly when visual issues arise during treatment to minimize potential vision damage. Our study also identified several AEs in the SOC of general disorders and administration site conditions, including injection site pain, injection site erythema, swelling, and rash at the injection site, as well as facial swelling. All these AEs have been documented in the medication instructions. Our research indicates that the risk of injection site reactions (including pain, swelling, and cyanosis) associated with dupilumab is significantly higher than that associated with tralokinumab (21.3% vs. 15.6%, p<0.001). The exact pathogenesis of urticaria remains incompletely understood, but it typically involves the release of various mediators from mast cells, such as histamine, proteases, prostaglandins, leukotrienes, and cytokines ( ). Exfoliative dermatitis is a severe form of dermatitis that can be caused by a variety of factors, including underlying skin diseases, infections, and medications ( ). Therefore, the occurrence of exfoliative dermatitis in patients treated with tralokinumab may be related to underlying disease severity rather than to the treatment itself. Further research is required to elucidate the relationship between tralokinumab treatment and the risk of exfoliative dermatitis. These findings emphasize the necessity for dermatologists to enhance patient monitoring and education throughout the treatment process. Our results demonstrated that the median time to onset of tralokinumab-related AEs was 37 days, with most occurring within the first month of treatment. Comparative analysis with dupilumab revealed differential AE profiles: dupilumab had higher injection-site reaction reporting rates, while tralokinumab showed higher conjunctivitis and keratitis rates. These findings inform post-market safety monitoring and clinical decision-making by highlighting underrecognized tralokinumab-associated AEs requiring closer monitoring. However, results should be interpreted cautiously due to limitations in the FAERS database (reporting biases and underreporting) and the observational study design. This study generates hypotheses that require validation through well-designed clinical trials to confirm safety signals, establish causal relationships, and characterize tralokinumab’s safety profile. Prospective trials with rigorous designs and larger sample sizes are needed to determine the accurate AE incidence rates, while mechanistic studies should elucidate underlying pathways and risk factors.

documents.title: BAD guidelines for the management of atopic eczema in children

chunks.content: Background Food allergy affects 8% of US children, with peanut allergy (PA) being the most prevalent (2.2%) [ ]. The Learning Early About Peanut (LEAP) study demonstrated that early introduction of peanuts to infants reduces the likelihood of developing PA in high-risk infants [ , ]. Therefore, the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) published the 2017 Addendum Guidelines for the Prevention of Peanut Allergy (PPA) [ ]. The guidelines stated that infants aged 4–6 months should be screened for PA risk and receive peanut introduction recommendations according to their risk level. Infants at high-risk (with severe eczema or egg allergy) should have a peanut specific Immunoglobulin E test conducted and/or should be referred to an allergist before peanut-containing foods are introduced. Infants at low-risk (with no or mild/moderate eczema) should begin eating peanut-containing foods at around 6 months of age or according to family preferences or cultural norms. By adhering to these guidelines, pediatric clinicians may contribute to reducing the incidence of PA. Despite the potential benefits of PPA guideline adherence, a 2018 national survey of pediatricians reported that only 1/3 of pediatricians used the guidelines fully as published [ ]. Limitations of this survey include that it was conducted 1.5 years after the guidelines were released and that pediatricians more familiar with the guidelines may have been more likely to respond. In contrast, electronic health records (EHRs) enable observation of real-world, documented practices via structured (e.g., prescriptions, diagnosis codes) and unstructured data (e.g., outpatient clinical notes and hospital discharge summaries). PPA guideline adherence (appropriate peanut introduction recommendations based on risk level) and PA risk factors are commonly documented within clinical notes in EHRs. However, while structured EHR data lends itself to data processing and analytics, the complexity of unstructured data poses a significant challenge because of the use of shorthand and variations in terminology and syntax. These challenges increase when studying data across practice sites and networks, with different note template formats and EHR interfaces. Manual labeling and extraction of information from an extensive volume of clinical text can be laborious, costly, and subject to human error. Therefore, clinical Natural Language Processing (NLP), a specialized application of NLP techniques to understand clinical notes, may be a valuable tool for analyzing and interpreting unstructured medical datasets from EHRs [ ]. NLP has proven to be useful in many healthcare applications [ – ] and is effective in identifying patients with food allergy based on well-child care (WCC) visit notes [ ]. In a pharmacovigilance study, one hour spent developing an NLP system reduced 20 hours of manual chart review; the time saved allowed the study team to focus their manual chart review on the 25% of the cohort that needed it [ ]. NLP can be used to compare free text data documented during standard clinical care across randomized controlled trial arms. For PA prevention, a multifaceted intervention was developed to support pediatric clinician adherence to the PPA guidelines. The Intervention to Reduce Early (Peanut) Allergy in Children (iREACH) trial included clinician education, an EHR integrated clinical decision support (CDS) tool in 4- and 6-month WCC visits, and follow-up EHR prompts in 9- and 12-month WCC visits. Clinicians in the control arm did not receive study-specific education or tools. A two-arm, cluster-randomized, controlled clinical trial was designed to evaluate the effectiveness of the intervention to increase pediatric clinician adherence to the PPA guidelines and decrease the incidence of PA. The pragmatic design of the iREACH trial meant that pediatric clinicians generated study data within the context of standard clinical practice, as recorded in the EHR. The iREACH trial design has previously been published [ ]. The purpose of this work is to describe the development of an NLP pipeline across three practice networks to identify peanut introduction recommendations and severe eczema. This work supports measurement of the iREACH trial’s primary outcome of pediatric clinician adherence to the PPA guidelines. Lurie Children’s Pediatric Practice Research Group (PPRG), AllianceChicago (Alliance), and PPRG-Peoria. Ann & Robert H. Lurie Children’s Hospital’s Data Analytics and Reporting team served as the data coordinating center and was responsible for developing and implementing the NLP pipeline. The networks included federally qualified health centers (Alliance), as well as independent (PPRG), hospital-owned (PPRG), and health care system-owned practices (PPRG-Peoria). Practice sites were randomized into control ( n = 14) and intervention ( n = 16) groups. During 18-month periods from November 2020 to October 2022, pediatric clinicians’ EHR data were extracted from 4- and 6- month WCC visits, for measurement of the primary outcome. Practice sites were randomized into control ( n = 14) and intervention ( n = 16) groups. Patient data The study database, a central data repository for the iREACH trial (Fig. ), included structured patient data such as demographic variables, visit types, visit diagnoses, problem lists, and medications. A common data dictionary was established to ensure that extract, transform, and load (ETL) processes generated interoperable data with standardized variable names, formats, and permissible values across all data sources. Clinical notes were also collected. Clinical notes were almost exclusively in English; however, a small number of clinical notes contained Spanish text. Clinical notes from PPRG-Peoria and PPRG (both based on Epic ) were structurally different from those of Alliance (based on Centricity). Notes from PPRG-Peoria and PPRG had a combination of free and templated text in sections, with some discrete data elements, including those generated via the CDS, inserted as text. Conversely, notes from Alliance were compilations of named data elements that required a text synthesis step to create narrative style notes that were similar to those from the other networks. The NLP processing focused on clinical notes related to the 4- and 6- month WCC visits only. Clinical notes were associated with a “note type,” and the use of these labels varied across the networks. At PPRG, 96% of the clinical notes for these visits from the start of the trial (11/2020) through 11/2022 were labeled as progress notes or patient instructions. All other note types (e.g. addendum notes, assessment and plan notes, confidential notes, nursing notes, and telephone encounters) were excluded from the NLP processing. At Alliance, 88% of the clinical notes were labeled as “office notes.” At PPRG-Peoria, 81% of the clinical notes were labeled as progress notes or patient instructions. Since the study team had less experience with clinical notes from Alliance and PPRG-Peoria, all note types from these networks were included in the NLP processing. NLP pipeline An NLP pipeline was developed to process clinical notes using CLAMP (Melax Technologies, Inc., Houston, Texas), a comprehensive NLP software package that facilitates recognition and encoding of clinical information within textual data [ ]. Developers can construct a customized NLP pipeline by selectively choosing components that manage NLP tasks such as sentence detection, tokenization, part-of-speech tagging, text chunking, and biomedical named entity recognition. By implementing a set of rules, multiple annotations related to these named entities were enhanced to create more meaningful and easily identifiable concepts. This process involved enriching the initial annotations produced by the NLP system, making them more comprehensive and contextually relevant. For example, when the NLP system identified a term related to peanut introduction or severe eczema, the implemented rules allowed for more information to be added to the annotation, such as the context in which the term was used or its relationship to other medical conditions mentioned in the text. This augmentation helped in transforming raw data into structured, clinically meaningful concepts that were easily recognized and then were used in downstream analyses. Finally, association rules were applied to detect the presence of, negation of, or irrelevant reference to key concepts. NLP pre-processing The initial phase of the NLP pipeline involves pre-processing all clinical notes to ensure accurate processing. Clinical notes often contained special characters that can cause misinterpretation by the NLP system. To address this, unnecessary characters (such as double spacing, leftover XML tags, or XML strings) were eliminated, while the semantic integrity of the clinical notes was preserved. The goal was to find any pertinent text that documented: (1) having discussed peanut introduction and/or (2) that peanut products were already in the infant’s diet; both scenarios were considered clinician adherence to the PPA guidelines. To achieve the goal, a named entity dictionary was established, encompassing all relevant peanut products. The peanut product had to be clearly defined, and not in general terms such as “food” or “allergenic foods.”]. The dictionary included: “peanut," "nut butters," "PB" (for peanut butter), and commercial products used for early peanut introduction, such as peanut powders and puffs. Peanut product concepts were then linked to a recommendation concept by creating another dictionary with keywords which included “recommend,” “introduce,” “expose,” “try,” and “discuss.” These two dictionaries were used to find the two concepts (“peanut product” and “recommendation”) together in a sentence. Peanut product concepts were then linked to a recommendation concept by creating another dictionary with keywords which included “recommend,” “introduce,” “expose,” “try,” and “discuss.” These two dictionaries were used to find the two concepts (“peanut product” and “recommendation”) together in a sentence. For example, “introduce peanut products if low risk.” While having the two distinct concepts indicate a peanut recommendation was made, it was not always necessary or relevant to have both. To account for situations in which (1) templated patient instruction text included a solid, strongly implied peanut introduction recommendation, or (2) peanut products were already in the infant’s diet, exceptions were made to the aforementioned two-concept rule. Examples include this templated instruction wording -- “there is no evidence that further delaying the introduction of highly allergenic foods (such as eggs, nut products, fish, and shellfish) beyond 6 months old will have any impact on whether or not your child develops food allergies” -- and that peanut products already had been introduced -- “Interval History: rash on abdomen after spoonful one.” These exceptions allowed the study team to identify more recommendations. NLP severe eczema Identification of severe eczema (or “atopic dermatitis”) in the text notes was necessary to categorize the risk of PA and to apply the PPA guidelines to determine clinicians’ adherence. The study team and subject matter experts defined severe eczema and formulated a comprehensive algorithm. Our definition of severe eczema was informed by the NIAID guidelines but was adapted to reflect how eczema severity is documented in the EHR. First, keywords that were dispositive and that limited the text from further consideration were defined. For example, if a healthcare provider classified eczema as “severe,” no further analysis of the text was necessary. Similarly, if the provider classified the eczema as “moderate” or “mild,” the eczema in that note was not characterized as “severe.” In cases where eczema was not characterized as “severe,” “moderate,” or “mild,” the NLP analyzed the note for descriptions of the physical examination of the skin. The NLP looked for the following keywords (or variants thereof) as descriptions of the eczema: “crusting,” “scaly,” “thickening,” “lichenification,” “oozing,” and “scabbing”. Presence of any of these descriptions was categorized as severe eczema if the structured data in the iREACH trial database’s medication table included any severe eczema-relevant medication (Fig. ). The list of medications was defined by clinical experts from the research team. Certain topical medications (such as hydrocortisone ≥ 2.5%, other steroids like desonide and triamcinolone in any form or strength, or calcineurin inhibitors like tacrolimus) or related oral medications were indicative of severe eczema. Topical creams with 1% hydrocortisone (typically an over-the-counter medication) were not considered to be a medication indicative of severe eczema. Finally, exclusions were applied to seborrheic dermatitis (cradle cap), a common infant scalp condition consisting of patches with oily, yellow scales or crusts. Unlike eczema, seborrheic dermatitis is not a risk factor for PA. If seborrheic dermatitis and eczema were mentioned in the same sentence, descriptions of the eczema were evaluated separately from the seborrheic dermatitis. NLP iterative development process The NLP algorithms for peanut recommendation and severe eczema underwent multiple iterations during development to enhance their performance. The development of the NLP was organized into three main phases: exploratory, training, and validation (Fig. ). In the training phase, the remaining two networks (Alliance and PPRG-Peoria) were also included. Random samples of 400 patients from PPRG and 100 each from Alliance and PPRG-Peoria who had 4- or 6-month WCC visits from 2020 to 2022 were used for the training sets. The first version of the NLP algorithm that applied to all networks was developed using knowledge from the pilot studies and these training sets. Iterative improvements followed, incorporating additional training datasets from PPRG, Alliance, and PPRG-Peoria ( n = 400 each), with continuous review by subject matter experts. In the validation phase, a gold standard dataset (Gold 1) was created from PPRG ( n = 856), Alliance ( n = 360), and PPRG-Peoria ( n = 284) patients who had 4- or 6-month WCC visits in 2020 to 2022 and had not been included in the training datasets. Each note in the Gold 1 dataset was evaluated by two trained chart reviewers to determine the presence of a peanut recommendation and severe eczema. The NLP algorithm from the training phases was applied to the Gold 1 dataset to assess performance. A second validation dataset (Gold 2) was created. Gold 2 was also composed of patients who had 4- or 6-month WCC visits in 2020 to 2022 (PPRG ( n = 216), Alliance ( n = 131), and PPRG-Peoria ( n = 53). Additionally, this dataset was built to include equal numbers of patients with and without eczema diagnosis codes. Eczema and related skin conditions were identified in the problem list data associated with the visit using the following ICD-10 diagnosis codes: atopic dermatitis (L20.8, L20.9, L20.81, L20.82, L20.83, L20.84, L20.89), contact dermatitis (L25.9), seborrheic dermatitis (L21.8, L21.9), and dyshidrotic eczema (L30.1). Two trained chart reviewers determined the presence of peanut recommendations and severe eczema in each note. NLP chart review process During the exploratory and training phases of the NLP development, narrative charts were reviewed by experts to refine the model. However, in the validation phase, a more systematic evaluation of the narrative charts was conducted by trained chart reviewers, including domain experts. These reviewers applied a structured and consistent approach to review the accuracy and reliability of the NLP model, providing a more thorough and rigorous assessment compared to the earlier stages. Results from the chart review were recorded in a project-specific data abstraction form, which was displayed alongside the narrative information from the chart for easy reference. For Gold 2 (not Gold 1), in addition to clinical narrative notes, reviewers were given a yes/no flag based on medication table data, showing whether the child had been prescribed severe eczema medication on-or-before the date of the 4- or 6-month WCC visit note being reviewed. Discrepancies in the chart reviewers’ assessments were resolved by discussion between two members of the study team (co-authors LB and MR). Results Infant characteristics were comparable across the two datasets (Gold 1 versus Gold 2). However, across networks, there was variability in race, ethnicity, and insurance type, owing to the network locations and types. The percent of infants with eczema or related skin conditions at 4- or 6- month WCC visits ranged from 0 to 69%. Few infants had egg allergy at 4- or 6- month WCC visits (0–1%). Infant characteristics are presented in Table . The iterative development process of the rule-based NLP algorithm led to two significant revisions: NLP Algorithm v1 and NLP Algorithm v2. NLP Algorithm v2 was a notable improvement over NLP Algorithm v1, with further refinement of the rules for identifying peanut recommendations and severe eczema. NLP Algorithm v1 was validated on the Gold 1 dataset, and NLP Algorithm v2 was validated on the Gold 2 dataset. The performance of these NLP algorithms for peanut recommendation is summarized in Table . NLP Algorithms v1 and v2 for peanut recommendation performed well in each practice network. In the Gold 1 dataset, NLP Algorithm v1 achieved precision values ranging from 0.82 to 0.99 and recall values ranging from 0.96 to 0.98, indicating its ability to accurately identify true positive cases. In the Gold 2 dataset, NLP Algorithm v2 had precision values ranging from 0.91 to 1 and recall values ranging from 0.63 to 0.98. NLP Algorithm v2 exhibited a higher F-measure in the networks combined, but did not outperform NLP Algorithm v1 in all instances. For example, in the PPRG Peoria dataset, NLP Algorithm v2 had an F-measure of 0.74 (precision = 0.91, recall = 0.63) while NLP Algorithm v1 had an F-measure of 0.89, (precision = 0.82, recall = 0.97). The performance of the NLP algorithms for identifying severe eczema is summarized in Table . Severe eczema was not common among infants; the number of true cases of severe eczema in the Gold 1 and Gold 2 datasets was low ( n = 67 in Gold 1 and n = 12 in Gold 2), with considerable variability across networks. In the Gold 1 dataset, NLP Algorithm v1 achieved an overall precision value of 0.62 and recall value of 0.81, while NLP Algorithm v2 demonstrated an overall precision value of 0.52 and recall of 0.92 in the Gold 2 dataset. In the Gold 1 dataset, NLP Algorithm v1 achieved an overall precision value of 0.62 and recall value of 0.81, while NLP Algorithm v2 demonstrated an overall precision value of 0.52 and recall of 0.92 in the Gold 2 dataset. The Gold 2 dataset had no true positive severe eczema cases in the PPRG-Peoria network to evaluate. In the Gold 1 dataset, NLP Algorithm v1 for identifying severe eczema demonstrated varied performance across different networks. While it exhibited high specificity and negative predictive value (NPV), indicating its ability to accurately identify true negative cases, its precision and recall were lower. For instance, in the PPRG network, the algorithm achieved a precision of 0.51 and recall of 0.84, resulting in an F-measure of 0.64. In the Alliance network, the F-measure, precision, and recall were all 0.64. In the PPRG-Peoria network, the algorithm achieved a higher F-measure of 0.88 with a precision of 0.90 and recall of 0.86. NLP Algorithm v2, in the networks combined, had higher recall and lower precision. In the PPRG network, Algorithm v2 achieved a precision of 0.64 and a recall of 1, resulting in a higher F-measure of 0.78. However, in the Alliance network, the algorithm showed lower precision (0.44) and recall (0.8), resulting in a lower F-measure of 0.57 than in Algorithm v1. In post-processing, structured data from the iREACH CDS system was used to enhance performance. Specifically, we incorporated the peanut recommendation and severe eczema CDS flags (if a clinician had entered that a peanut recommendation was made this visit or previously, or if a clinician had entered that the patient had severe eczema). This CDS data was not displayed to the reviewers. The NLP model’s performance in the analyses that integrated the CDS flags is detailed in the Appendix Tables and . This CDS-enhanced version of the NLP was used in the iREACH randomized clinical trial analyses. A manual review of the actual iREACH trial cohort’s clinical notes was conducted to ensure the highest level of accuracy and reliability for severe eczema in the analyses in the trial. While automated NLP processes can handle large volumes of data efficiently, manual review allowed for a more thorough examination of the results, to help to identify situations or nuances that automated NLP approaches missed. This approach provided an added layer of validation in the iREACH trial. Discussion In this study, two NLP algorithms were developed to identify (a) peanut recommendations and (b) severe eczema as characterized by pediatric clinicians in clinical notes. Through iterative refinement, two high-performing iterations of these algorithms were crafted, which were subsequently validated in expert-reviewed datasets. Both algorithms performed well on identifying peanut recommendation and were considered acceptable to use in the iREACH trial. The rare occurrence of severe eczema was more difficult to discern using NLP. Therefore, to finalize the analytic data for the trial, the study team manually reviewed all clinical notes that had an NLP indication of possible severe eczema, based on NLP algorithm v2. The study findings demonstrate success in identifying peanut recommendations. The pipeline performed well enough to apply to the large corpus of 4- and 6-month WCC visit notes of 18,480 infants in the iREACH trial. Considering the volume of notes in the trial, an NLP approach was the only viable solution to identify visits at which pediatric clinicians recommended the introduction of peanut products. The successful development of an NLP pipeline to extract this recommendation is a primary contribution of this study which can be replicated in other pragmatic clinical trials. However, identifying cases of severe eczema posed significant challenges, as reflected by lower performance metrics. It is important to consider that the prevalence of eczema among all children is estimated to be 13%, with severe eczema estimated to be 7% of all eczema cases [ ]. Therefore, the rarity of severe eczema in the Gold 1 and 2 datasets was expected. Also, severe eczema is much more complex as a concept than peanut recommendation is. Some patients have severe skin manifestations at one visit but respond swiftly to treatment and have only mild disease at a subsequent visit. Although the performance metrics suggested that the trial results should not rely exclusively on the NLP algorithm, the NLP approach was helpful in identifying infants with possible severe eczema, which prompted further manual chart reviews to exclude false positives. Although the performance metrics suggested that the trial results should not rely exclusively on the NLP algorithm, the NLP approach was helpful in identifying infants with possible severe eczema, which prompted further manual chart reviews to exclude false positives. Variability in clinical practice across different networks presents a significant challenge in consistently identifying and treating severe eczema. There appears to be a lack of consensus among pediatric clinicians on how to define severe eczema, possibly stemming from differences in interpreting clinical guidelines or the inherent complexity of the condition itself. This variability is consistent with a previous study of resident physicians that demonstrated inconsistency in assessing eczema severity [ ]. Therefore, establishing consensus on diagnostic criteria (such as by using a Validated Investigator Global Assessment for Atopic Dermatitis (vIGA-AD) [ ]) and on treatment strategies is essential for ensuring optimal patient care across diverse healthcare settings. The variability in clinical practice and its documentation may have contributed to differences in the performance of NLP across the networks. NLP algorithms also can inherit biases present in the source data, leading to outputs with less accuracy for certain patient groups. Data may reflect persistent racial and ethnic disparities in the diagnosis of eczema and treatment of severe eczema [ – ]. There is an understanding in the field that the diagnosis of eczema needs to better encompass patients of all “shades of skin.” [ ] For this reason, a picture-based vIGA-AD scorecard was developed that reflected diverse skin tones and was provided to clinicians in the intervention arm of the iREACH trial; [ ] nevertheless, there may have been differences in eczema diagnoses across skin tones in both arms of the iREACH trial, which may have created biases within the clinical notes data used by the NLP. Other differences in clinical note writing across networks also pose a challenge for rule-based NLP algorithms. While rule-based NLP has been used in many studies to extract information from clinical notes, its rigid structure may have difficulty accommodating diverse formatting. Clinical notes also may contain language and terminology that vary significantly between different specialties or institutions [ , ]. To address this limitation, more advanced methods such as large language models (LLM) offer promising alternatives. LLMs have demonstrated superior adaptability to variations in text formatting and language usage, which makes them better suited to navigate the complexities of clinical notes sourced from diverse healthcare settings. There are several other limitations of this study. First, the use of NLP to measure the iREACH outcomes was based on the assumption that clinicians document clinical recommendations to patients in progress notes. A recommendation to the parent/caregiver to introduce peanut products may not always be documented by a clinician. Additionally, the CDS in the EHR made it easier to document peanut recommendations in the intervention group. Opportunities for documentation also differed between Epic a nd Centricity EHR systems. The structure of Centricity, with its “obs” terms (succinct text in named data elements that had to be compiled by the project team into narrative style notes), seemed to offer Alliance clinicians fewer opportunities to document in narrative form. Therefore, peanut recommendations and severe eczema were more likely to be identified among intervention patients in Alliance. Conclusions Further research is warranted, especially in the identification of severe eczema, to improve and validate NLP findings and to explore the potential benefits of adopting an NLP algorithm in clinical practice. Overall, this study demonstrates the utility of an NLP approach in helping measure clinical trial outcomes in pragmatic studies.
